issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly interprets the manipulation as probing memory at different post-stimulus delays, but in Experiments 1, 2, and 4 the response is not collected at those times. What varies is the delay to the spatial cue; participants respond only after a later second display at a fixed time. Thus the key construct of 'memory delay' is misoperationalized. This undermines claims that memories are sampled at 0.5 s versus 3 s and that illusions increase simply because more time has elapsed.
issues.quote: After this, the memory display was presented for 0.25 seconds, a blank screen, only containing the fixation cross was presented for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition). Then the cue was presented for 0.25 seconds... 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds... After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options

issues.description: Because the manipulated interval is the delay to a retro-cue, the short condition gives participants earlier information about which location will be tested. That can improve performance by allowing prioritization/protection of the cued item or dropping uncued items, independent of any transformation of memory content. Therefore the short-versus-long comparison is confounded with retro-cue benefits and cannot be cleanly interpreted as memory distortion increasing over time.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 2 would be supported if high confidence illusory reports become more prevalent with longer memory delays... After this, the memory display was presented for 0.25 seconds, a blank screen... was presented for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition). Then the cue was presented for 0.25 seconds

issues.description: The study attributes changes to time-based decay and sometimes to interference, but all experiments present a second letter display before response. Without a condition that omits this second display at test, the design does not isolate pure passage-of-time effects from retroactive interference or source confusion caused by the second display itself.
issues.quote: 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds (participants were instructed to ignore this second display). After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options

issues.description: The central causal argument is too strong. An increase in mirror-confusion errors over the retention interval does not show that initial perception was accurate or that the illusion originated only in memory. Initial perceptual misencoding can coexist with later retrieval/decision biases, and later cueing or interference can magnify the behavioral expression of an earlier ambiguity. The manuscript treats a non-exclusive pattern as decisive evidence against perceptual contributions.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.description: The paper treats high confidence as necessary and sufficient evidence that an error reflects a genuine illusory memory rather than guessing. That is not warranted. Confidence is itself a metacognitive judgment that can be biased by fluency, response preferences, feedback, or overconfidence; high-confidence errors do not by themselves demonstrate access to a stored false memory trace.
issues.quote: Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly dismisses response bias without having modeled bias separately from memory strength. A tendency to choose canonical real letters could increase when memory is weak, producing exactly the reported pattern. Without signal-detection, multinomial, or hierarchical choice models, the data cannot distinguish altered memory content from biased decision/readout.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: The conclusion that 'world knowledge' drives the effect is not uniquely supported. Pseudo-letters may simply be harder to encode, verbalize, rehearse, or retain than real letters; the 'mirrored' feature may be lost over time. No control stimuli matched for familiarity/nameability are included, and no articulatory-suppression or discriminability control is used. Therefore the observed asymmetry does not isolate top-down world knowledge from asymmetric encoding and maintenance demands.
issues.quote: high confidence errors occurred mainly for pseudo-to-real letter memories, and much less often for real-to-pseudo-letter memories, indicating that visual similarity is not the primary cause of this memory-bias. Instead ‘world knowledge’ (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.description: The manuscript claims support for predictive processing, but the experiments do not discriminate predictive-processing accounts from simpler alternatives such as feature loss, category-based reconstruction, verbal-coding asymmetries, or response bias. The theoretical conclusion is therefore stronger than the design permits.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.description: Participants were excluded post hoc based on having too few high-confidence trials in design cells. This criterion is arbitrary, depends on the very construct being tested, and is not justified with a preregistered rule. Such outcome-contingent exclusions can materially inflate apparent effects among retained participants.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.description: The exclusions are large and selective. In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants were removed, and included versus excluded participants differed sharply in high-confidence responding. This means the analyzed sample is a selected subgroup of more confident participants, limiting validity and potentially biasing effect sizes.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions (range: 24.6 – 95.8, sd: 13.3). Excluded participants had on average 15.7% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 0.4 – 38.8%, sd: 9.5).

issues.description: Zero counts in some cells were handled by listwise deletion of participants rather than by a model appropriate for sparse binomial/multinomial data. This discards informative data and can bias results toward participants with more responses in the focal categories.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.description: The analyses use repeated-measures ANOVA on aggregated error percentages/relative occurrence, despite the data being bounded proportions arising from discrete trial counts that differ across subjects and cells after exclusion/collapsing. This ignores the binomial/multinomial sampling structure and unequal precision of estimates. Trial-level mixed-effects logistic or multinomial models would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to 'high confidence trials' but does not clearly specify which confidence levels counted as high confidence in each experiment, despite changing the response scale across studies. Without the threshold, the analyses cannot be reproduced or properly interpreted.
issues.quote: After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4). ... error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA

issues.description: Experiment 1 reports 40 participants remaining after training exclusion, but later states that the analysis included 23 participants and only 5 were excluded. Those numbers are mutually inconsistent; 40 to 23 implies 17 not 5 exclusions. This prevents the reader from knowing the actual analyzed sample.
issues.quote: The remaining 40 participants (28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years)... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Experiment 1 gives two incompatible descriptions of the confidence scale. The figure caption states a 1–4 scale, whereas the procedure describes only two boxes (1–2). This inconsistency affects interpretation of the high-confidence filter and comparability across experiments.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty). ... participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: In Experiment 1 the target and its mirrored counterpart were presented with markedly different probabilities depending on target type, and real targets were more common overall. This creates substantial opportunity for experiment-wide learning and response-frequency bias, complicating interpretation of the observed asymmetry. Although Experiment 2 addresses this, it remains a serious problem for Experiment 1 and for claims of consistency across all four experiments.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%. If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.description: The text states that for non-illusory errors only Memory Delay mattered and that Target Type did not. Table 4 reports the opposite pattern: Memory Delay shows evidence against inclusion (BFincl = 0.064), while Target Type shows extremely strong evidence for inclusion (BFincl = 39110.895). This is a critical inconsistency in the reported statistical results.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42... ). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets... / Table 4 ... Memory Delay ... BFincl 0.064 ... Target Type ... BFincl 39110.895

issues.description: The cue-color manipulation in Experiment 2 lacks a valid manipulation check. An open-ended post-experiment questionnaire is not sensitive evidence that participants learned or used the contingency, especially when the effect is claimed to be implicit. In addition, the two colors differed substantially in luminance, so color could also affect attention/visibility rather than expectation. As a result, the null conclusion about transient expectations is not interpretable.
issues.quote: both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2). ... Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential stopping based on a 'critical t-test', but the final analyses are Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs. Stopping on one statistic and reporting another creates analytic flexibility unless fully preregistered and justified. No details are given about the Bayes-factor prior, whether the stopping rule used included/excluded participants, or whether the final model was fixed in advance.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayesian ANOVAs and Bayes factors but does not specify crucial modeling details such as prior distributions/scales, prior odds, or any sensitivity analyses. Because Bayes factors depend on these settings, the results are not fully evaluable or reproducible from the manuscript alone.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online on participants' own laptops with brief presentations and fine mirror-orientation discriminations, yet the manuscript provides no control or calibration for screen size, refresh rate, browser timing, viewing distance, or keyboard/mouse latency. This is a substantial validity concern for a task whose effects depend on precise visual presentation and short retention intervals.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time... given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: The data come largely from University of Amsterdam students, many in first-year psychology courses, performing tasks on highly overlearned Latin letters. Conclusions are nevertheless framed broadly about STM, perception, and memory traces in general. The findings may depend strongly on literacy, alphabet familiarity, age, education, and task context, so the general claims exceed the sampled population and stimuli.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum... All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.description: The discussion contains contradictory claims. One passage correctly states that iconic memory was not tested; another immediately generalizes to 'all stages of STM'. The broader claim is unsupported by the presented experiments.
issues.quote: Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM... The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research

issues.description: The critique of fuzzy trace theory is logically inverted. The manuscript says FTT predicts that high similarity should facilitate false memories, then claims the present data are inconsistent because the mirrored counterpart and target are extremely similar and false memories are abundant. That pattern is, if anything, consistent with the stated prediction. This weakens the theoretical argument against FTT.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: The key comparison pits 'illusory errors' against a composite of qualitatively different 'other errors'. In Experiment 2, those other errors can include selecting another studied letter pair or a completely unstudied pair, which reflect different processes (e.g., swap errors vs novel intrusions). Collapsing them into one category weakens the interpretation that a main effect of Error Type uniquely indexes memory illusions.
issues.quote: The response screen consisted of 6 letters, 3 real letters and their pseudo counterparts. 2 pairs of letter/pseudo-letters had been part of the memory display... and 1 pair had not been part of the memory display. ... error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors)

issues.description: Experiment 1 allowed only participants who exceeded 75% accuracy on a separate cued change-detection task with rectangles to enter the main experiment. This preselection may yield a non-representative sample with unusually strong visual memory/attention, yet the main conclusions are generalized to STM broadly. The training task is also not a direct validation of mirrored-letter discrimination.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training. We adopted this procedure to ensure that all participants were motivated, and possessed a minimal proficiency at visual memory tasks.

issues.description: The manuscript extends findings from mirrored letters to visual percepts in general and to broad implications for vision research. Those extrapolations are speculative because no non-letter stimulus sets were tested here, and the mechanism may depend on literacy-specific familiarity and naming.
issues.quote: Secondly, it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general. This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.
